captions: Part three. Triggers.
A workflow does nothing until an event wakes it
up. Let's meet the events.
The on key accepts dozens of events. Here are
the ones you'll use most.
push and pull request — the heart of CI.
workflow dispatch — a manual Run button.
schedule — run on a timer.
release — when you publish a version.

issues and issue comment — to automate project
management.

workflow run — start one workflow after another
finishes.

And repository dispatch — let an outside system
trigger
you through the API.
One workflow can listen to several events at once.

Usually you don't want every push to trigger
everything.
So events take filters.

branches limits runs to certain branches. tags does
the
same for tags.
paths is the powerful one. It says: only run
if these files changed.
Watch. This push changed a readme and a doc.
Neither matches src slash star star, or package dot
json — so the workflow is skipped.
The next push touched a source file. Match —
the workflow runs.

For pull requests, types narrows it further: opened,
synchronize,
labeled, and so on.
Good filters save minutes, money and noise.

The schedule trigger uses cron syntax. Five fields:
minute,
hour, day of month, month, and day of week.
Thirty, two, star, star, one to five means: at
two thirty, Monday to Friday.
One catch — the time is always UTC. In
India, two thirty UTC is eight AM IST.
Scheduled runs use the default branch, can start a
few minutes late when GitHub is busy, and can't
run more often than every five minutes.

In public repos, schedules pause after sixty days
without
activity.

Use them for nightly builds, dependency checks,
reports and
cleanup.
workflow dispatch adds a Run workflow button to the
Actions tab.
Better still, it takes inputs. Here we ask for
an environment — staging or production — and a
dry run checkbox.
GitHub renders them as a small form. You pick
values, click Run, and the workflow reads them from
the inputs context.

It's perfect for one-click deploys, database
migrations, and anything
a human should start on purpose.
You can trigger the same thing from a terminal,
too, with gh workflow run.
